785.title: Arjuna's austerities
785.hook: Arjuna fights the hunter with everything he has and loses, then lays a garland before Shiva and sees it on the hunter's head
785.howItsDone: Devotees of Shiva retell Arjuna's defeat and recognition as a story of the god meeting his worshipper in disguise, and the garland found on the hunter's head is a remembered detail of the story.

segments.voice: Yesterday Arjuna's austerities brought him face to face with a hunter, and he picked a fight. Did you give someone one breath before deciding who they were? Day seven hundred eighty-five.

Everything Arjuna has, he throws at the hunter. This is the great archer, carrying the bow Gandiva and quivers the epic describes as never running out. He looses a storm of arrows. And the hunter simply stands there and takes them, unhurt, the way a mountain takes rain. Arjuna shoots and shoots, and then something happens he didn't expect. He reaches back, and the quiver is empty. Today, the fight Arjuna loses, and what he does next.
screen: `A STORM OF ARROWS.` → `THE HUNTER STANDS UNHURT.` → `THE QUIVER IS EMPTY.`

segments.voice: So Arjuna fights with whatever is left. He strikes with the end of his bow, and the hunter snatches the bow away. He draws his sword and brings it down on the hunter's head, and the sword breaks. He fights with his fists. The two of them wrestle, and the hunter presses him so hard that Arjuna can't breathe, and he falls senseless to the ground. Everything his austerities built, the strength, the focus, the warrior's pride, has failed. And then, coming to, bruised and beaten, Arjuna does the thing he came to the mountain for in the first place. He stops fighting and turns to worship. He shapes an altar from earth, honors Shiva upon it, and lays a garland of flowers there. And when he looks up, he sees the garland. It's on the hunter's head. That's the moment of recognition. The flowers he offered to Shiva have arrived on the stranger he was trying to beat. Arjuna understands who has been standing in front of him all along, and he falls at Shiva's feet and asks forgiveness. And Shiva is pleased with him. Arjuna didn't win; in the telling, it's his courage in the fight that Shiva praises. Arjuna's austerities, it turns out, needed this last part. Fasting on air made him strong. Losing made him see. The god he was straining toward was right there, in a hunter he'd dismissed, and his own offering is what showed him.
screen: `THE BOW TAKEN, THE SWORD BROKEN.` · `ARJUNA FALLS SENSELESS.` · `A GARLAND LAID BEFORE SHIVA.` · then, large: `THE GARLAND ON THE HUNTER'S HEAD.`

segments.voice: Let yourself settle, and loosen anything you're holding: the jaw, the hands, the shoulders. Bring to mind something you've been fighting hard. A problem, a person, a part of yourself. Breathe in, and feel how tired the fight has made you. Breathe out, and set it down for a moment, the way Arjuna set down his weapons and picked up flowers. You don't have to give up. Just stop pushing for these few breaths. If you pray, you can offer that struggle in your prayer. If not, simply rest. The bell holds the time.
Arjuna's austerities. They end in a lost fight, an altar of earth, and a garland found on the head of the hunter who was Shiva.

786.title: Arjuna's austerities
786.hook: Shiva gives Arjuna his own weapon with a warning, the guardians of the world add theirs, and a chariot comes down for him
786.carry: use only as much as you need
786.howItsDone: In Hindu storytelling, Shiva's gift of the Pashupata weapon to Arjuna is remembered together with its warning, and the episode is honored by devotees of Shiva as a sign of the god's grace to a devoted seeker.

segments.voice: Yesterday Arjuna's austerities ended in a lost fight and a garland on the hunter's head. Your line was stop pushing, offer something instead. Did you stop pushing in one struggle, and offer something instead? Day seven hundred eighty-six.
screen: `ARJUNA'S AUSTERITIES.` · `THE GARLAND ON THE HUNTER'S HEAD.`

segments.voice: What does a god give a man who just tried to kill him? Arjuna is on his knees, bruised, asking forgiveness. The hunter's disguise has fallen away, and Shiva stands before him with Uma at his side. And the first thing Shiva does isn't a lecture. He hands back the bow. Gandiva, the one he snatched in the fight, is returned to Arjuna's hands. Then Shiva says: ask for what you want. Today, the gift at the end of Arjuna's austerities, and the warning that comes with it.
screen: `WHAT DOES A GOD GIVE?` → `SHIVA HANDS BACK THE BOW.` → `ASK FOR WHAT YOU WANT.`

segments.voice: There's no anger in Shiva at all. And he touches Arjuna, and his wounds and his exhaustion are gone. Then Arjuna asks for what he climbed the mountain for. He asks for Shiva's own weapon, the one called Pashupata. Shiva gives it to him, and teaches him how to use it. But he adds a warning, and it's the heart of the scene. This weapon, he says, must never be hurled at a human foe, and never at a weaker one. Used wrongly, it could destroy the world. Shiva's own weapon comes with Shiva's own limit. And then the sky fills with visitors. The guardians of the world arrive one after another: Varuna, lord of the waters; Kubera, lord of wealth; Yama, lord of death; each offering Arjuna a weapon of his own. Last comes Indra, the father who tested him in disguise at the start of all this. Indra tells him a chariot will come for him, to carry him up to Indra's own city, where he will receive more. So the whole arc of Arjuna's austerities comes into view. He set out holding a purpose, and wouldn't put it down. He burned with tapas until the mountain felt it. He met Shiva as a stranger, lost to him, and recognized him through his own offering. And what he receives at the end isn't only power. It's power with a rule attached, given by a god who first healed the man who had fought him.
screen: `SHIVA HEALS AND PRAISES ARJUNA.` · `THE PASHUPATA WEAPON.` · `NEVER AGAINST A WEAKER FOE.` · then, large: `THE GUARDIANS OF THE WORLD ARRIVE.`

Breathe in, and receive it as a gift. Breathe out, and hear Shiva's warning: never against someone weaker. Where might that strength need a limit? Let that question sit with you, no judgment, just attention. If you pray, you can give thanks for that gift and ask to use it well. The bell holds the time.

787.title: Arjuna's austerities
787.hook: in Indra's city, Urvashi comes to Arjuna's door at night, and he covers his eyes
787.carry: pause once before you follow it
787.howItsDone: The episode of Urvashi and Arjuna is told within the Vana Parva of the Mahabharata, and retellers often pair it with the later year in disguise, when the curse becomes Arjuna's cover.

segments.voice: Yesterday Arjuna's austerities ended on the mountain: Shiva healed him and gave him the Pashupata with a warning, and the guardians of the world added their weapons. Did you use only as much of the upper hand as you needed? Day seven hundred eighty-seven.

Arjuna is living in heaven. His brothers are still in the forest, and he is in Indra's city, learning the weapons of the gods. Indra has him learn music and dance as well, from the gandharva Chitrasena. Then one evening Indra notices how Arjuna's eyes follow the apsara Urvashi, and he sends word to her. So that night, dressed for him, she comes to his door. And the archer who stood alone on a mountain and fought a hunter who turned out to be Shiva does something Urvashi doesn't expect. He covers his eyes.
screen: `ARJUNA IN INDRA'S CITY.` → `URVASHI AT THE DOOR.` → `HE COVERS HIS EYES.`

segments.voice: In the telling, Arjuna speaks to her with great respect, and what he says surprises her. You are an elder of my own line, he tells her. Tradition says Urvashi was the mother of an ancestor of the Pandavas' house, so to Arjuna she stands where Kunti stands, or Indra's queen. He looked at her in the hall, he says, the way a child looks at an honored elder. Urvashi answers that the apsaras are free, that rules like his don't bind them. He doesn't move. And she is furious. She curses him: he will live among women as a dancer, without his manhood, and be thought little of. Arjuna goes to Chitrasena, and the story reaches Indra. And here the story turns. Indra isn't angry. He's pleased. He praises Arjuna's self-control, and then he tells him that this curse will serve him. When the brothers must live hidden, unrecognized, he will spend that time as a dancer among women, and no one will look for the great archer there. When that time is over, the curse is over too. So look at what austerity means in this story. On the mountain it was fasting, standing, enduring. Here it's a door, a night, and a no. The same discipline, carried into a palace full of pleasures. The epic doesn't treat the curse as a reward for virtue, exactly. It treats it as something stranger: a wound that becomes a hiding place. And that closes Arjuna's austerities. He went up for weapons. He comes down with weapons, a teacher's music, and a disguise he doesn't know he'll need.
screen: `"YOU ARE AN ELDER OF MY LINE."` · `URVASHI'S CURSE.` · `INDRA: IT WILL HIDE YOU.` · then, large: `AUSTERITY CARRIED INTO A PALACE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath find its own pace. Sooner or later a small pull may come: to shift, to scratch, to check the time, to think about dinner. If it comes, don't fight it, and don't follow it. Just notice it rise, the way Arjuna noticed the knock at the door, and let it pass like a breath going out. Then come back to the breath. If it comes again, notice again. If you pray, you can offer that small no as part of your prayer. If not, simply let each pull come and go. The bell holds the time.
Arjuna's austerities. They began on a mountain with fasting and ended in a palace with a closed door, and a curse that would one day hide him.

788.title: Nala and Damayanti
788.hook: Yudhishthira asks if any king was ever more unlucky, and a sage begins the story of Nala and a golden swan
788.carry: a story can hold a grief
788.howItsDone: The story of Nala and Damayanti is told within the Vana Parva of the Mahabharata, by the sage Brihadashva to Yudhishthira, and it is also retold on its own.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Arjuna's austerities: a door in Indra's city, a refusal, and a curse that would one day hide him. Your line was pause once before you follow it. When did a pause change something for you? Day seven hundred eighty-eight.

Back in the forest, Arjuna is gone, and his brothers miss him. Yudhishthira is the one who threw the dice, and he can't stop going over it. So when a sage named Brihadashva visits the camp, Yudhishthira asks him a question that sounds like a complaint and is really a plea. Has there ever been a king more unlucky than me? The sage doesn't argue with him. He doesn't give him a lecture. He tells him a story. There was a king, he says, who also lost his kingdom at dice. His name was Nala. And the story begins, of all places, with a bird.
screen: `YUDHISHTHIRA'S QUESTION.` → `"MORE UNLUCKY THAN ME?"` → `THE SAGE TELLS A STORY.`

segments.voice: Nala is the king of the Nishadhas: handsome, learned, truthful, and a master with horses. Far away, in Vidarbha, lives Damayanti, the daughter of King Bhima, and the story praises her beauty in line after line. The two have never met. But people talk, and each keeps hearing about the other, and each begins to love someone they have never seen. One day, in a garden, Nala catches a swan with wings that shine like gold. The swan speaks. Let me go, it says, and I'll praise you to Damayanti so well she'll think of no one else. Nala lets it go. The swan flies to Vidarbha and lands among Damayanti and her friends, and when she reaches for it, it speaks to her of Nala. Damayanti's answer is simple: say the same of me to him. So a bird carries love back and forth between two people who live in different kingdoms. Then Damayanti grows pale and quiet, and her father notices. He decides it's time for her swayamvara, the ceremony where a princess chooses her own husband, and kings start arriving from every direction. Now step back and see why the sage tells this story here. Yudhishthira wants to know if his suffering is the worst there has ever been. The sage answers with a love story that starts in a garden. He's asking Yudhishthira to listen all the way to the end. A story can hold a grief long enough for someone to see it from a little distance. So we'll stay with Nala and Damayanti for a while, the way Yudhishthira did.
screen: `NALA, KING OF THE NISHADHAS.` · `DAMAYANTI OF VIDARBHA.` · `A GOLDEN SWAN CARRIES THE NEWS.` · then, large: `A STORY TO HOLD A GRIEF.`

789.title: Nala and Damayanti
789.hook: the gods want Damayanti too, and they make Nala carry their proposal to her
789.carry: a human sign can make you kinder
789.howItsDone: The scene of Damayanti choosing the human Nala among the gods is part of the Nala story in the Vana Parva of the Mahabharata, which a sage tells to Yudhishthira in the forest.

segments.voice: Yesterday a sage began the story of Nala and Damayanti for a grieving king, and a golden swan carried love between two people who had never met. Your line was a story can hold a grief. Did a story reach you when advice couldn't? Day seven hundred eighty-nine.

Nala is on the road to Damayanti's swayamvara when he meets some travelers who are not travelers at all. They are Indra, Agni, Varuna and Yama, the gods themselves, and they're headed to the same ceremony for the same reason. They ask Nala for a favor, and he says yes before he knows what it is. Then they tell him. Go to Damayanti, they say, and ask her to choose one of us. So the man who loves her is now the messenger for his rivals. And they happen to be gods.
screen: `TRAVELERS ON THE ROAD.` → `THE GODS ASK A FAVOR.` → `NALA BECOMES THEIR MESSENGER.`

segments.voice: Nala protests, but he has given his word, and he keeps it. By the gods' power he walks unseen past the guards and into Damayanti's rooms. She and her friends are startled by the handsome stranger, and she asks who he is. He tells her: I am Nala, and I come as a messenger from the gods. Choose one of them. Damayanti doesn't hesitate. She has already given herself to Nala, she says, in her heart. Then she finds a way through. Let the gods come to the ceremony, she tells him, and you come too, and I'll choose you in front of them, so no blame falls on you. Nala carries her answer back honestly, word for word. Then the day comes. Damayanti walks into the hall with her garland, and she sees Nala. And next to him, another Nala. And another. The gods have taken his shape, and she can't tell them apart. So she does the one thing left. In her heart she bows to the gods and asks them, by the truth of her vow, to show her who is who. And they do. The gods show the marks of the gods: no sweat on their skin, eyes that don't blink, garlands still fresh, no dust on them, feet not quite touching the ground. And one of them casts a shadow. His garland is wilting. There's dust on him, and sweat, and he blinks. She chooses the one who is only human. So the two of them meet in the middle of the same test: Nala keeping his word against his own heart, and Damayanti keeping hers by asking the gods for the truth.

790.hook: Kali arrives too late for the swayamvara, waits for one small lapse, and enters Nala
790.carry: one small habit of care, done on purpose

On their way home from the wedding, the gods meet latecomers on the road. One is Kali, the spirit of strife and bad luck, with his companion Dvapara. Kali is hurrying to the swayamvara to win Damayanti. The gods tell him he's missed it: she has chosen Nala. Kali doesn't take it well. He swears to get into Nala, to take his kingdom, to part him from his wife, and he tells Dvapara to get into the dice. Then he does something quietly frightening. He waits.
screen: `THE LATECOMERS ON THE ROAD.` → `KALI'S OATH.` → `HE WAITS.`

segments.voice: Nala, the story says, is a good king. He rules well, he offers sacrifices, he loves Damayanti, and they have children. Kali can't find a way in. So he watches, and he waits, for a long, long time. Then one evening Nala relieves himself and, before he sits down for his evening prayers, forgets to wash his feet. That's all. One small lapse in a careful life. And through it, Kali enters him. Kali goes to Nala's brother, Pushkara, and whispers to him: challenge Nala at dice, and you'll win his kingdom. And Nala, with Kali inside him, can't say no to the challenge. They play. Nala loses. They play again. He loses again. His ministers come to the door to stop him. The people of the city come. Damayanti herself comes. He won't even look up. So Damayanti does the one thing in her power. She calls the charioteer, Varshneya, and has him take their children away to her father's house, where they'll be safe. Then Nala loses everything else. And here Pushkara asks for one more stake: Damayanti. Nala won't do it. He stands up, takes off his ornaments, and walks out of his own city in a single cloth. Damayanti walks after him. Remember who is listening. Yudhishthira, the king who also played and couldn't stop, sits there in the forest and hears all of this. The sage doesn't point at him. He doesn't have to. A story about someone else lets a person look at his own life without being shamed.

791.title: Nala and Damayanti
791.hook: in the forest, birds fly off with Nala's last cloth, and that night he cuts the one they share
791.howItsDone: In the Vana Parva of the Mahabharata, the sage Brihadashva tells Yudhishthira how Nala left Damayanti sleeping in the forest; in this scene the couple are parted.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nala and Damayanti lost everything: one small lapse, a brother's dice, the children sent to safety, and a king walking out of his city in a single cloth. Your line was one small habit of care, done on purpose. What small habit did you do on purpose? Day seven hundred ninety-one.

Outside the city, Nala and Damayanti are hungry. Nobody will help them; Pushkara has made sure of that. Then Nala sees birds on the ground with wings that shine like gold, and he thinks: food. He throws his one cloth over them to catch them. And the birds rise into the air, carrying the cloth away with them. From the sky they speak. We are the dice, they tell him. We came to take even this. Now a king stands in the forest with nothing on at all.
screen: `GOLDEN BIRDS ON THE GROUND.` → `HE THROWS HIS LAST CLOTH.` → `"WE ARE THE DICE."`

segments.voice: So Damayanti shares hers. The two of them wrap themselves in her single garment and keep walking. As they go, Nala keeps pointing out the roads. This one leads south. That one goes to Vidarbha, your father's country. He says it more than once. Damayanti hears what he isn't saying, and she answers it. Why are you showing me the roads? she asks. I won't leave you. If you want, we'll both go to my father's house, and he'll honor you. Nala says he won't go back to her family like this. They come to an empty rest house, and they lie down on the bare ground, and Damayanti, exhausted, falls asleep. Nala can't. Kali is still inside him, and his grief is pulling at him. He thinks: if I go, she'll go home to her people. If I stay, she'll suffer with me. He finds a sword lying nearby. He cuts the cloth in half, as gently as he can, so she won't wake. Then he goes. Then he comes back and looks at her. Then he goes again. Then he comes back. The story lets him go back and forth, torn between love and Kali, until at last he leaves. Look at the week we've walked. It started with Arjuna on a mountain and in Indra's city, choosing restraint when he could have taken what was offered. It ends with Nala, not in his right mind, cutting a cloth in the dark. Both of these men are being tested. Tonight, one of them, with Kali still inside him, can't hold on. The sage keeps telling the story anyway, because it isn't over.
screen: `ONE CLOTH FOR TWO.` · `"WHY SHOW ME THE ROADS?"` · `THE SWORD AND THE CLOTH.` · then, large: `HE GOES, AND COMES BACK, AND GOES.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind someone who has stayed with you when it would have been easier to go. You don't have to name the hard time. Just see their face. Breathe in, and let yourself remember that they stayed. Breathe out, and send them a quiet thank you, wherever they are. If a time comes to mind when you left, or someone left you, let it be there too, without judging it. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer. If not, simply stay with the memory of someone who stayed. The bell holds the time.
Vastra, the one cloth they shared. Carried off by birds at first, then this single garment, until a husband cuts it in the dark and leaves, and comes back, and leaves.
Your line: notice who stays beside you. Today, notice who stays beside you, and let them know you've noticed. Day seven hundred ninety-one.
